Assistant Professor in Natural Resource Economics
Nine-month tenure-track appointment in Logan, Utah
50% teaching, 45% research, 5% service | Start date to be determined


Position Summary
Utah State University’s Department of Agricultural and Resource Economics seeks an Assistant Professor in Natural Resource Economics, prioritizing water economics and policy relevant to Utah and the Intermountain West.
Responsibilities
• Teach undergraduate and graduate courses, face-to-face or online, in environmental and natural resource economics, benefit-cost or policy analysis, applied microeconomics, or quantitative methods, according to departmental needs.
• Develop a nationally recognized research program in water economics and policy, including conservation, allocation, agricultural water use, or policy evaluation. Related work on land use, public lands, ecosystem services, energy, or climate adaptation may complement this focus.
• Publish high-quality peer-reviewed research and communicate findings to academic and policy audiences. Collaborate with state partners and Extension colleagues on policy briefs or decision tools.
• Seek external funding and pursue disciplinary and interdisciplinary collaboration within and beyond the university.
• Mentor undergraduate and graduate students, serve on graduate supervisory committees, and contribute departmental, college, university, and professional service consistent with rank and appointment.
Minimum Qualifications
A Ph.D. in economics, applied economics, agricultural economics, natural resource economics, or a closely related field by the start date; demonstrated potential for productive research and effective undergraduate and graduate teaching; and strong quantitative, written, and oral communication skills.
Preferred Qualifications
Expertise in water economics and policy relevant to Utah and the Intermountain West; high-quality scholarship appropriate to career stage; potential for successful grant writing and interdisciplinary collaboration; face-to-face or online teaching experience and evidence of effectiveness; and potential to mentor graduate students and contribute to graduate program development.
